newsitem.title: USA: LIFFE official says concerned about Labour policy.
newsitem.headline: LIFFE official says concerned about Labour policy.

text.p: A tradition of self-regulation in London's financial community could be harmed if a new Labour government in Britain steps up regulation, a top industry official said on Thursday.

"Obviously, we're concerned with a change in policy," Daniel Hodson, chief executive of London Financial Futures and Options Exchange (LIFFE), said at an annual commodities and financial services law conference in Chicago.
"I think there will be an attack in policy on the borderline of self-regulation," he told a panel session on international regulation.
British Prime Minister John Major, whose Conservative Party has been lagging behind Labour by wide margins in opinion polls, must call an election by May next year.
"The feeling over here (in the United States) is that the borderline is moving in a positive direction toward self-regulation," Hodson said. "In England it's going the other way."

To date, the futures industry in Britain has thrived on self-regulation, co-existing with a high concentration of over-the-counter (OTC) markets, Hodson said. He noted that there was a lot of regulatory collaboration between the two.
By contrast, U.S. futures exchanges often complain they are losing business to OTC derivatives markets because of unfair regulatory burdens on them.
"In London, we don't see it that way at all," Hodson said. "We see it (OTC) as a complementary part of the structure."
Still, Chicago Board of Trade (CBOT) president Thomas Donovan, also speaking at the session, said there was a momentum in the U.S. to make the playing field more level.

A bill to amend the Commodity Exchange Act had been introduced and top officials from CBOT, Chicago Mercantile Exchange, National Futures Association and Futures Industry Association visited the Commodity Futures Trading Commission (CFTC) together recently, Donovan said.
"This group going there with one common theme is unprecedented," he said.
The officials urged new CFTC chairman Brooksley Born to consider the cost-benefit ratio of regulations, specifically audit-trail requirements, and to simplify procedures to introduce new products.
CME president Bill Brodsky, also at the session, agreed there was increasing cooperation among U.S. exchanges in regulatory issues and cost-cutting.

LIFFE's Hodson said he welcomed moves toward self-regulation in the U.S., even though they might make his rivals more competitive, because an adverse U.S. regulatory move could set off similar measures in Britain.
Panelists added that a growing use of the Internet was causing new cross-border regulatory problems for authorities.
But they said the industry's future prosperity could hinge on such new technology and that authorities' approach to the matter remained to be seen.
